lead: A fully controlled converter fired beyond 90° gives a negative average voltage while its current keeps the same direction, so power flows from the DC side back into the AC supply: the converter inverts. This is how a DC drive brakes regeneratively, how an HVDC receiving station feeds power into the grid, and how a line-commutated converter returns the energy of a battery or a superconducting magnet. Inversion has a hard upper limit on α, set by the overlap and by the time a thyristor needs to recover; firing later than that causes commutation failure.
prereq: You need: continuous current and Vdc = Vd0 cos α from single-phase controlled rectifiers, and the overlap angle from effect of source inductance.

blocks.text: A thyristor bridge cannot reverse its current, so the only way to reverse power P = Vdc Id is to reverse Vdc. Three things are needed:

items: A fully controlled converter: a half-controlled bridge or a freewheeling diode clamps the output at zero and cannot invert.

A DC source in the load whose polarity drives current into the converter's positive terminal: a DC machine running as a generator (its field or armature reversed), a battery connected the other way, or the DC line of an HVDC link.
α between 90° and the limit α_max, with the current continuous, so that Vdc = Vd0 cos α is negative.

blocks.text: In steady state the averages obey Vdc = E + Id R, with E now negative and |E| > |Vdc|, so Id = (Vdc − E)/R > 0. The DC source supplies |E| Id, the resistance takes Id²R and the rest, |Vdc| Id, goes into the AC supply. In the V–I plane the converter has moved from quadrant I (rectifier) to quadrant IV (inverter).

When the incoming thyristor is fired at α, the outgoing one must hand over its current and then block. After the overlap ends at α + μ, the outgoing thyristor sees a reverse voltage only until 180°, where the two commutating voltages cross; after that its anode is positive again. That reverse-biased interval is the extinction angle (margin angle):
γ = 180° − (α + μ)   and it must satisfy   γ ≥ γ0 > ω tq
blocks.where: γ is the extinction angle in degrees; tq is the thyristor's circuit turn-off time in s; ω = 2πf in rad/s. On 50 Hz, tq = 100 µs is ωtq = 1.8°; γ0 is chosen larger than ωtq to leave a safety margin.

blocks.text: If γ is too short, the outgoing thyristor has not recovered when its voltage turns positive, so it conducts again. Current returns to it, the incoming thyristor turns off, and the DC source drives current straight through two thyristors of the same leg: the DC side is short-circuited and the current climbs. This commutation failure (an inverter fault) is why the firing angle in inversion is never taken to 180°.

Without overlap the limit is simply α_max = 180° − γ0. With source inductance the overlap also has to fit inside the half-cycle, and it grows with current. Put α + μ = 180° − γ0 into the overlap equation of the three-phase bridge, cos α − cos(α + μ) = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL):
cos α_max = 2ωLs Id/(√2 VL) − cos γ0;   Vdc = (Vd0/2)(cos α − cos γ) = −(Vd0 cos γ − ΔVd)
blocks.where: Vd0 = 3√2 VL/π and ΔVd = 3ωLs Id/π. For a single-phase bridge use 2ωLs Id/Vm on the right of the first equation.

blocks.text: So the heavier the current, the larger μ and the smaller α_max, and the less inverse voltage the converter can offer. A controller that holds α fixed would fail as soon as the current rose; HVDC inverters and regenerative drives therefore control γ directly (constant extinction angle control), computing the firing instant from the measured current.

examples.question: A single-phase fully controlled bridge on 230 V, 50 Hz brakes a DC machine regeneratively. The machine's EMF, connected for inversion, is E = −120 V and its armature resistance R = 2 Ω; the current is continuous and α = 120°. Find Vdc, Id and the power returned to the supply, and check the power balance.
steps: Id = (Vdc − E)/R = (−103.54 + 120)/2 = 8.23 A, positive as it must be.
Power into the AC supply = |Vdc| Id = 103.54 × 8.23 = 852 W.
Power from the machine = |E| Id = 120 × 8.23 = 988 W; loss in R = 8.23² × 2 = 136 W; 852 + 136 = 988 W.
examples.answer: Vdc = −103.5 V, Id = 8.23 A, 852 W returned to the supply.

examples.question: A three-phase bridge on 400 V, 50 Hz with Ls = 1 mH per phase works as an inverter with a minimum extinction angle γ0 = 15°. Find α_max, μ and Vdc at Id = 100 A, and α_max at Id = 20 A.
examples.answer: At 100 A: α_max = 148.7°, μ = 16.3°, Vdc = −491.8 V (49.2 kW returned). At 20 A the limit rises to 160.7°.

traps: Saying the current reverses in inversion. It cannot; the voltage reverses.
Claiming a half-controlled bridge can invert. Its diodes clamp the output at zero.
Writing the limit as α ≤ 180°. It is α + μ ≤ 180° − γ0, and μ depends on the current.
Taking γ0 equal to ωtq. A margin above the turn-off time is always added.
Forgetting the source: an RL load alone cannot keep a converter inverting in steady state, because its average voltage is Id R > 0.

quiz.q: Define the extinction angle of a line-commutated inverter.
quiz.a: γ = 180° − (α + μ): the angle during which the outgoing thyristor is reverse biased after the overlap, before its voltage turns positive again.

quiz.q: List the three conditions for a phase-controlled converter to invert.
quiz.a: A fully controlled converter; a DC source of suitable polarity to keep the current flowing; α above 90° (and below α_max) with continuous current.

quiz.q: Explain what happens in a commutation failure.
quiz.a: The outgoing thyristor has not recovered when its voltage becomes positive, so it carries current again; the incoming device turns off, two thyristors of one leg conduct, and the DC source is short-circuited through the bridge, so the current rises sharply.

quiz.q: A 50 Hz inverter uses thyristors with tq = 200 µs and a 5° safety margin. Ignoring overlap, find α_max.
A single-phase bridge on 230 V inverts at α = 150° with continuous current into a machine with E = −190 V and R = 1 Ω. Find Id and the power returned.
Why does a heavier DC current force a smaller firing angle in inversion?
quiz.a: The overlap needs a fixed volt-second area 2ωLs Id, so μ grows with Id. Since α + μ must stay below 180° − γ0, α_max falls: in the worked example from 160.7° at 20 A to 148.7° at 100 A.

beyond: Not for the exam. In HVDC links the rectifier station controls the current and the inverter station controls the extinction angle, and the meeting of their two characteristics fixes the operating point; this 'current margin' method is the classic HVDC control scheme. Superconducting magnets and large battery banks are discharged through line-commutated inverters the same way. Search for 'constant extinction angle control', 'HVDC current margin' and 'commutation failure HVDC'.

figure.caption: The second worked example’s bridge with γ0 = 15°. Overlap lowers the output by 6 V at 20 A and 30 V at 100 A, and each curve must stop where α + μ reaches 165°: at 160.7° for 20 A but already at 148.7° for 100 A.

spec.aria: Plot of average output voltage against firing angle from 0 to 180 degrees. A dashed cosine for no overlap, a curve 6 volts lower for 20 amperes ending at 160.7 degrees, and a curve 30 volts lower for 100 amperes ending at 148.7 degrees, beyond which a shaded band is marked commutation failure. The left half is labelled rectifier, the right half inverter.
